messages.author: 23e9c489ea8b313a
messages.subject: Nonlinear regression using stan
parts:
I am writing a second edition of my 1988 Wiley book with Don Watts on nonlinear regression.  I thought it would be a good idea to mention McMC as an inference technique for such models, although the emphasis will be on profiling the residual sum of squares to create likelihood regions.  A common problem in nonlinear regression inference using the likelihood is that the model loses sensitivity to changes in parameter values at extremes.  In Bayesian terms this means that using an improper prior can result in an improper posterior.

My first attempt at fitting a simple model is 
library(rstan)
options(show.signif.stars=FALSE)
PurTrt <- subset(Puromycin, state=="treated", -state)
summary(pm1 <- nls(rate ~ SSmicmen(conc, Vm, K), PurTrt))
confint(pm1)
mmstan <- '
data {
 int<lower=1> N;
 real rate[N];
 real conc[N];
}                            # based on profiling the sum of squares
parameters {
 real lVm;
 real lK;
 real<lower=0> sd;
}
transformed parameters {
 real<lower=0> Vm;
 real<lower=0> K;
 Vm <- exp(lVm);
 K <- exp(lK);
}
model {
 real mu[N];
 for (i in 1:N)
      mu[i] <- Vm * conc[i]/(K + conc[i]);
 rate ~ normal(mu, sd);
 sd ~ gamma(0.0001, 0.0001);
 lVm ~ normal(0, 10); // use proper priors for model parameters
 lK ~ normal(0, 10);
}
'
(samp <- stan(model_name="Purtrt", model_code=mmstan, data=c(PurTrt, N=nrow(PurTrt))))


I used the logarithm of the parameters Vm and K as these parameters must be positive.  

An alternative version is to use the parameters Vm and K but constrain them
mmstan1 <- '
data {
    int<lower=1> N;
    real<lower=0> rate[N];
    real<lower=0> conc[N];
}
parameters {
    real<lower=0> Vm;
    real<lower=0> K;
    real<lower=0> sd;
}
model {
    real mu[N];
    for (i in 1:N) 
        mu[i] <- Vm * conc[i]/(K + conc[i]);
    rate ~ normal(mu, sd);
    sd ~ gamma(0.0001, 0.0001);
    Vm ~ normal(0, 1000) T[0,]; // use proper priors for model parameters
    K ~ normal(0, 10) T[0,];
}
'
(samp1 <- stan(model_name="Purtrt1", model_code=mmstan1, data=c(PurTrt, N=nrow(PurTrt))))


The second version seemed more stable and also produced much larger n_eff values for the parameters.  Nevertheless the results were still not as close to the mle's as I would have expected.

Are there any suggestions for improvements in my model specification?  I'm not altogether sure of appropriate priors for the standard deviation, sd, and for the nonlinear model parameters, Vm and K, so please tell me if I have made a faux pas there.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Nonlinear regression using stan
parts: Hi Doug,

On Tuesday, October 9, 2012 4:36:42 PM UTC-4, Douglas Bates wrote:
An alternative version is to use the parameters Vm and K but constrain them

Stan does have the lognormal distribution, so I think the .stan code below with lognormal priors on the constrained-to-be-positive quantities should be conceptually equivalent to the first version you gave. There could be small computational differences in addition to random differences, but let us know if there are any substantial differences.
 
mmstan2 <- '

data {
    int<lower=1> N;
    real<lower=0> rate[N];
    real<lower=0> conc[N];
}
parameters {
    real<lower=0> Vm;
    real<lower=0> K;
    real<lower=0> sd;
}
model {
    real mu[N];
    for (i in 1:N) 
        mu[i] <- Vm * conc[i]/(K + conc[i]);
    rate ~ normal(mu, sd);
    sd ~ gamma(0.0001, 0.0001);

Vm ~ lognormal(0, 10); // use proper priors for model parameters
    K ~ lognormal(0, 10);
}
'
(samp2 <- stan(model_name="Purtrt1", model_code=mmstan2, data=c(PurTrt, N=nrow(PurTrt))))


Ben

messages.subject: Re: Nonlinear regression using stan
parts:
Thanks for the suggestions, Ben.

I have a couple of style questions, mostly related to the need to specify the length of vectors in addition to the vectors themselves.  It is common to have stanzas like

data {
   int<lower=1> N;
   real<lower=0> rate[N];
   real<lower=0> conc[N];
}

in a stan model (although sometimes in the manuals the declaration of N is "int<lower=0> N;", which doesn't make sense to me as you can't really expect to do much with 0-length vectors).

When passing data from R and even when reading data from an R dump file you determine the length of the vector as part of the parsing of the arguments.  Is it reasonable to try to find a way to avoid needing to specify the vector lengths so that a data.frame can be passed as the data?  In my example I take advantage of the fact that a data frame is also a list and use the c(<data.frame>, N=nrow(frm)) construction to get the vectors and their length into a list.  Of course, it would not be difficult to write a short R function to do that packaging of the vectors and their length but it seems like it should be possible to finesse that issue.

One point on terminology, although it is probably too late to change this and it may be a holdover from the BUGS/JAGS world, you recommend the .Rdata extension for files in the R dump format.  Typically in R the .Rdata extension is used for binary save files, not R dump files.  This could end up being confusing.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Nonlinear regression using stan
parts: Hi Doug,

On Tuesday, October 9, 2012 5:49:17 PM UTC-4, Douglas Bates wrote:
Thanks for the suggestions, Ben.

I have a couple of style questions, mostly related to the need to specify the length of vectors in addition to the vectors themselves.  It is common to have stanzas like
data {
   int<lower=1> N;
   real<lower=0> rate[N];
   real<lower=0> conc[N];
}
in a stan model (although sometimes in the manuals the declaration of N is "int<lower=0> N;", which doesn't make sense to me as you can't really expect to do much with 0-length vectors).

I can see how this would be confusing from an R perspective where almost everything is a vector in some sense, but some vectors happen to be of length one. But from a C++ perspective, N is a scalar while rate and conc are std::vectors. In other words, the above parses as:

class doug_model : public prob_grad_ad {
private:
    int N;
    vector<double> rate;
    vector<double> conc;
public:
...

I suppose it is valid to write in a .stan file

data {
  int<lower=0> N[1];
}

to get a std::vector called N of length 1. But it isn't necessary and you would have to remember to write N[1] subsequently. We put some effort into making Stan "work" with 0-length vectors and 0x0 matrices. But I wouldn't rely on it working, and I can't think of a situation where it wasn't a mistake on the user's part.

When passing data from R and even when reading data from an R dump file you determine the length of the vector as part of the parsing of the arguments.  Is it reasonable to try to find a way to avoid needing to specify the vector lengths so that a data.frame can be passed as the data?  In my example I take advantage of the fact that a data frame is also a list and use the c(<data.frame>, N=nrow(frm)) construction to get the vectors and their length into a list.  Of course, it would not be difficult to write a short R function to do that packaging of the vectors and their length but it seems like it should be possible to finesse that issue.

It sounds like a reasonable request, but I'm not immediately seeing how to make it work on the C++ side. Maybe the C++ file stan() generates could #define NROW__  and let this .stan syntax

data {
  real<lower=0> rate[]; // implicitly using NROW__ as the length
  real<lower=0> conc[]; // implicitly using NROW__ as the length
}

be valid. Andrew would probably like it and Bob would probably hate it. We'll see.

One point on terminology, although it is probably too late to change this and it may be a holdover from the BUGS/JAGS world, you recommend the .Rdata extension for files in the R dump format.  Typically in R the .Rdata extension is used for binary save files, not R dump files.  This could end up being confusing.

This is confusing. In Appendix D.3, footnote 2, of the Stan manual we note this confusion, but I can't remember if there was a reason we use .Rdata in the examples.

Ben

This is the right edge behavior if zero-length data results
in the parameters being sampled from the prior. But if
the model specifies an operation only defined on non-empty
vectors, such as mean or sd, then the model will raise an
error if there's a zero-length input, so it'd be better to
catch the error early by putting it in the data declaration.

> I realize that N is needed in the C++ code, I am just advocating trying to find a way to make it easier to specify it in
> R when using rstan.

Andrew was saying exactly the same thing. And
also advocating writing a reader for (multiple joined)
files CSV data, which would be very helpful in
the typical (multilevel) regression setting.

Any suggestions on how we could figure out what N
should be? The way all the readers are set up in C++,
we need to know the length of vectors to read. (The
underlying reason is the conversion from the unconstrained
parameter vector to the constrained parameters used in
the model.)

>
> to get a std::vector called N of length 1. But it isn't necessary and you would have to remember to write N[1]
> subsequently. We put some effort into making Stan "work" with 0-length vectors and 0x0 matrices. But I wouldn't rely
> on it working, and I can't think of a situation where it wasn't a mistake on the user's part.
>
> When passing data from R and even when reading data from an R dump file you determine the length of the vector
> as part of the parsing of the arguments. Is it reasonable to try to find a way to avoid needing to specify the
> vector lengths so that a data.frame can be passed as the data? In my example I take advantage of the fact that
> a data frame is also a list and use the c(<data.frame>, N=nrow(frm)) construction to get the vectors and their
> length into a list. Of course, it would not be difficult to write a short R function to do that packaging of
> the vectors and their length but it seems like it should be possible to finesse that issue.
>
>
> It sounds like a reasonable request, but I'm not immediately seeing how to make it work on the C++ side. Maybe the
> C++ file stan() generates could #define NROW__ and let this .stan syntax
>
> |
> data {
> real<lower=0> rate[]; // implicitly using NROW__ as the length
> real<lower=0> conc[]; // implicitly using NROW__ as the length
> }
> |
>
> be valid. Andrew would probably like it and Bob would probably hate it. We'll see.

I'll reserve judgment until I can figure out how
something like this could be made to work!

I have no issue with the language doing more inference
on data structures and types as long as it's well defined and
not too confusing (like I don't think we should go to C++-style
template metaprogramming!).

You might be able to use something like rate_len and conc_len,
but then we lose the constraint that they're the same length.
I want that to be declared in the data in the model. I believe
it makes the models easier to read because the bounds of all
the data structures are right there.

It can be a bit more of a pain to get a model working, but
I also believe it pays the cost back in debugging effort.

Other people have very different preferences for typing in
their programming languages. I hear some people even like Perl
and Python and R programming :-)

> This is confusing. In Appendix D.3, footnote 2, of the Stan manual we note this confusion, but I can't remember if
> there was a reason we use .Rdata in the examples.

Fixing this is on the to-do list -- the footnote's a stop-gap.
This was my fault for not understanding the R conventions.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Nonlinear regression using stan (zero data bounds, .Rdata suffix, inferring array length)
parts:
On Wednesday, October 10, 2012 12:48:44 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>     It sounds like a reasonable request, but I'm not immediately seeing how to make it work on the C++ side. Maybe the
>     C++ file stan() generates could #define NROW__  and let this .stan syntax
>
>     |
>     data {
>        real<lower=0> rate[]; // implicitly using NROW__ as the length
>        real<lower=0> conc[]; // implicitly using NROW__ as the length
>     }
>     |
>
>     be valid. Andrew would probably like it and Bob would probably hate it. We'll see.

I'll reserve judgment until I can figure out how
something like this could be made to work!

I was imagining that the above would parse as

        rate = std::vector<double>(NROW__,double(0));
        if (!context__.contains_r("rate"))
            throw std::runtime_error("variable rate not found.");
        vals_r__ = context__.vals_r("rate");
        pos__ = 0;
        size_t rate_limit_0__ = NROW__;
        for (size_t i_0__ = 0; i_0__ < rate_limit_0__; ++i_0__) {
            rate[i_0__] = vals_r__[pos__++];
        }
        ...

Basically, my imagined rule would be "if the length is unspecified in the .stan file, assume it is NROW__ in the .cpp file". But the logic probably would need to be fleshed out more to deal with corner cases, and even then, I am assuming you and Andrew would disagree.

For a variety of reasons, it might be good to have a block in the .stan file that was pasted literally into the .cpp file after the #includes but before anything else. Something like

literal code {
#define N 1000
}
data {

real<lower=0> rate[N];
  real<lower=0> conc[N];
}
could compile faster than the usual

data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  real<lower=0> rate[N];
  real<lower=0> conc[N];
}

because the compiler could allocate a bunch of stuff at compile time instead of runtime. Although that would mean the binary wouldn't work if you wanted to pass different samples to it, and there would be no bounds on N to check.

The literal code block could also be used to define implicit functions if we supported that some day.
 
Ben
